questions.prompt: A user reports they can see an Account record on their screen, but can't edit one specific field on it. Which layer should you check first, and why does the fact they can see the record at all already narrow down the problem?
options: Field-level security — seeing the record at all already confirms both their object access and record-level access passed, which narrows the problem to one specific field
Organization-wide defaults — seeing the record proves OWD must be too restrictive for this object
The role hierarchy — seeing the record means a hierarchy-based grant must be missing somewhere
Profile CRUD permissions on the object — seeing the record means the object-level permission itself must be the problem
questions.explain: Lesson 1 splits every access question into object/field access and record-level access, and the two stack independently. If a user can see the record on screen at all, both their object-level Read permission and every record-level mechanism (OWD, hierarchy, sharing) already passed — the only thing left that could block editing one specific field is field-level security on that field.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about CRUD and the View All / Modify All permissions, per Lesson 2.
options: Create, Read, Edit, and Delete are independent permissions — a user can have Read and Edit without Create or Delete
View All grants Read access to every record of the object, regardless of sharing settings or ownership
Modify All grants Edit and Delete access to every record of the object, the same kind of override as View All
Object permissions like CRUD are stored on a role, not on a profile or permission set
Standard profiles have had fully editable CRUD on standard objects since Winter '21, the same as custom profiles
questions.explain: CRUD permissions are independent of each other, and View All/Modify All are a separate administrative category that bypasses record-level sharing entirely for Read, or Edit and Delete. CRUD permissions live on profiles and permission sets, never on a role. Standard profiles have been mostly locked down, not fully editable, on standard-object CRUD since Winter '21 — custom profiles are where that configuration actually happens.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: every Salesforce user has exactly one ________, assigned the moment their user record is created, which also sets their login hours and password policy.
questions.explain: Lesson 3 establishes the profile as the one mandatory, single-per-user setting — required at creation, never additive the way permission sets are, and the only place login hours and password policy live.

questions.prompt: A Permission Set Group contains Permission Set A, which grants Edit access on a sensitive field. An admin wants to suppress just that one grant, without removing Permission Set A from the group and without affecting anywhere else Permission Set A is assigned standalone. What should they do?
options: Mute that specific permission inside the permission set group
Remove Permission Set A from the group entirely
Edit Permission Set A directly to uncheck Edit on the field
Create a second permission set that revokes Edit on the field
questions.explain: Muting is the one exception to permission sets being additive-only, and it's narrow by design: it suppresses a specific grant inside one group's own calculation without touching the member permission set anywhere else it's assigned. Removing the permission set or editing it directly would affect every other assignment of it too.

questions.prompt: Match each Field-Level Security term or screen to what it actually is, per Lesson 5.
left: System fields like Owner, Created By, Last Modified By
Set Field-Level Security (from the field itself)
right: Can the user change the field's value — requires Read Access first
Shows every permission set and profile granting object access, each with its own Read/Edit checkboxes for one field, reachable from Object Manager
Can the user see the field's value at all
Greyed-out, locked checkboxes that FLS structurally can't restrict
questions.explain: Read Access controls visibility of a field's value; Edit Access controls changing it and requires Read Access first. System fields like Owner and Created By show as greyed-out, locked rows because FLS can't restrict them. Set Field-Level Security, reached from the field in Object Manager, shows every permission set and profile's Read/Edit checkboxes for that one field in one place.

questions.prompt: A user's profile does not grant Edit access on the Industry field, but a permission set assigned to them does. What is their actual effective access to that field, and why?
options: Edit access — effective access is the union of every granted source, and any single grant is enough, regardless of what other sources stay silent on
No edit access — the profile's silence functions as an explicit deny that overrides the permission set
Edit access, but only if the permission set was assigned to the user after the profile was
Read-only access — when sources conflict, Salesforce defaults to whichever is more restrictive
questions.explain: Lesson 6's union rule means there's no 'deny' at this layer and no 'most restrictive wins' — effective access is the sum of the profile plus every assigned permission set, and any one source granting Edit is enough. A profile that simply doesn't mention a permission isn't denying it; it's just silent.

questions.prompt: A profile should let Sales Reps update existing Opportunity records, but should never let them create new Opportunities or permanently delete existing ones. Which combination of object permissions on Opportunity is correct?
options: Read and Edit checked; Create and Delete unchecked
Read, Edit, and Create checked; Delete unchecked
Read, Edit, and Delete checked; Create unchecked
Only Read checked
Create, Read, Edit, and Delete all checked
Only Edit checked, with Read unchecked
questions.explain: CRUD permissions are independent (Lesson 2): the requirement needs visibility and updates but explicitly withholds both creation and permanent removal, which maps exactly to Read and Edit checked with Create and Delete unchecked.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B matches the correct combination in every respect except one extra checkbox: it also grants Create, which lets reps add brand-new Opportunity records — exactly the one capability the requirement says to withhold.

questions.prompt: An object needs to be fully editable by every internal employee, but completely invisible to portal, community, and guest users outside the org. Which Organization-Wide Default setting correctly achieves this?
options: Default Internal Access: Public Read/Write; Default External Access: Private
Default Internal Access: Public Read/Write; Default External Access: Public Read/Write
Default Internal Access: Public Read Only; Default External Access: Private
Default Internal Access: Private; Default External Access: Private
Default Internal Access: Public Read/Write; Default External Access: Public Read Only
Default Internal Access: Controlled by Parent; Default External Access: Private
questions.explain: Lesson 7 splits OWD into two separate columns. Internal needs to be fully editable, so Internal Access must be Public Read/Write; External needs to be completely hidden, so External Access must be Private — the most restrictive of the three core levels.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E keeps the same correct Internal setting but sets External Access to Public Read Only instead of Private. Public Read Only still lets every portal, community, and guest user view the record — it only blocks editing — so the object is not actually invisible outside the org the way the requirement demands.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Organization-Wide Defaults recognize three core access levels — Private, Public Read Only, and ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 7 names the three core OWD levels as Private, Public Read Only, and Public Read/Write, where everyone can view and edit records they don't own.

questions.prompt: Rep A and Rep B are peers who both report to the same Regional Manager in the role hierarchy. Rep A owns an Opportunity. Does Rep B gain any access to it through the role hierarchy alone?
options: No — the hierarchy only flows upward to the manager and whoever is above them, never sideways between peers
Yes — peers who share the same manager automatically share each other's records
Yes, but only Read access, never Read/Write
It depends on whether Grant Access Using Hierarchies is enabled specifically for Rep B
questions.explain: Lesson 8 is explicit that the role hierarchy flows up the tree, not across it. Rep B gains nothing from being Rep A's peer; only the Regional Manager, and anyone above them, gets the automatic rollup.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about sharing rules, per Lesson 9.
options: Owner-based sharing rules share records based on who owns them
Criteria-based sharing rules share records based on field values on the record, regardless of who owns it
A sharing rule can share records directly with one specific named individual user
Sharing rules can narrow access that OWD or the role hierarchy already grants
Adding a sharing rule to an object whose OWD is already Public Read/Write internally accomplishes nothing new
questions.explain: Owner-based and criteria-based are the two sharing-rule types, sharing to a public group, a role, or a role and its subordinates — never an individual. Sharing rules only ever widen access, never narrow it, and they accomplish nothing on an object that's already Public Read/Write, since there's nothing left to add.

questions.prompt: A recruiter manually shares a job application record with a colleague covering for them, then transfers ownership of that record to a third person. What should you expect to happen to the colleague's manually-shared access?
options: It's removed — Salesforce clears manual shares granted by the previous owner when a record's ownership changes
It stays exactly as it was, since manual shares are permanent once granted
It automatically upgrades to Read/Write
It transfers to the new owner instead of staying with the colleague
questions.explain: Lesson 10 calls this out as a real gotcha: manual shares granted by the previous owner are removed when ownership changes, unless the new owner is already above the old one in a covering hierarchy — with no error or notification calling it out.

questions.prompt: Match each Account/Opportunity/Case Teams concept to what it actually is, per Lesson 11.
right: Divides revenue credit among team members — a related but distinct feature from record access
A free-text label describing what a team member actually does on the record
Read Only or Read/Write granted per member, independent of profile, permission sets, or the role hierarchy
A pre-configured standard team added to new records automatically in one click, instead of rebuilt each time
questions.explain: Team Role is a free-text description of what a member does; Access Level is the Read Only/Read-Write grant set independently per member; Default Team lets a standing team get pulled onto new records automatically; Splits allocate revenue credit and are a separate feature from team-based record access, even though they live on the same Opportunity.

questions.prompt: A support manager wants two things: everyone on the team to be able to see escalated cases for visibility, and unworked cases to sit somewhere until an agent claims one. Which mechanism solves which need, per Lesson 12?
options: A public group provides the shared visibility; a queue provides the holding location for unworked cases
A queue provides the shared visibility; a public group provides the holding location
A single public group can do both jobs on its own
A single queue can do both jobs on its own
questions.explain: Public groups answer 'who should be able to see this' — the recipient a sharing rule points at. Queues answer 'who's responsible for working this' — a holding location unworked records sit in until someone claims one. They solve different jobs even though both are 'a bunch of users.'

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an object whose Organization-Wide Default shows ________ instead of Private, Public Read Only, or Public Read/Write has no independent sharing model of its own — its access is inherited entirely from its parent record.
questions.explain: Lesson 13 covers Controlled by Parent on objects like Contact and Asset — there's no separate sharing model to configure, because access to the child is whatever access to the parent record already is.

questions.prompt: At a sales org where two reps can legitimately both sell to the same account — unlike Meridian Outfitters, where territories never overlapped — would Private OWD plus a plain role hierarchy alone correctly model access?
options: No — Private OWD with a role hierarchy only grants automatic rollup to managers above the owner; overlapping peers with no reporting relationship between them would still need an owner-based or criteria-based sharing rule
Yes — the role hierarchy alone automatically grants access to any legitimate co-seller
No — the only fix for overlapping territories is switching OWD to Public Read/Write
Yes — Private OWD prevents overlapping territories from ever becoming an access problem in the first place
questions.explain: Lesson 14's own check-yourself question points at this: Private OWD plus hierarchy handles 'up the chain' access, but two peers who both legitimately co-sell the same account aren't related by the hierarchy at all — exactly the gap sharing rules exist to close, the same pattern Meridian used for its co-sold national accounts.

questions.prompt: Harbor Point Support sets Case OWD to Public Read Only, while Meridian Outfitters set Opportunity OWD to Private. What business difference actually explains the different choice?
options: Harbor Point's cases are worked by whichever agent is available via shared queues, not owned by one fixed person the way Meridian's sales territories are
Case data is inherently less sensitive than Opportunity data, so it can always default to a more open setting
Public Read Only is simply Salesforce's unchangeable default for the Case object
Harbor Point has far fewer total users than Meridian, so broader defaults are safer
questions.explain: Lesson 15 is explicit that OWD isn't a style preference — it follows how the business actually works. A service org built around shared, unowned queues needs broader read access than a sales org built around fixed individual territories, which is the opposite instinct from Meridian's design in Lesson 14.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Harbor Point Support's escalation design, per Lesson 15.
options: Escalation adds the next tier to the case team rather than reassigning the case
A criteria-based sharing rule grants the Tier 3 queue Read/Write on Critical cases before anyone manually escalates
Reassigning a case to Tier 2 preserves the Tier 1 agent's original context automatically
A queue functions like a special kind of public group that serves as a holding location for unowned records
Support Managers are placed above all three tiers in the role hierarchy to gain their broad case access
questions.explain: Harbor Point keeps prior-tier agents on the case team with Read Only instead of reassigning, which is exactly why reassignment (which loses context) is avoided. A criteria-based rule routes Critical cases to Tier 3 with Read/Write proactively. A queue is described as a special kind of public group. Support Managers get their broad access through a public-group sharing rule, not by sitting in a role hierarchy above the tiers.

questions.prompt: A user has View All on Account at the profile level, and a restriction rule is also configured on Account for a group that includes this user. What does the user actually see?
options: Everything View All grants — restriction rules cannot narrow access for users who have View All or Modify All on the object
Only the records matching the restriction rule's criteria, since restriction rules always take priority over object permissions
Nothing — View All and an active restriction rule cancel each other out
Whichever of the two is more restrictive for that specific record
questions.explain: Lesson 16 states this directly: restriction rules can only narrow access a user would otherwise have, and users with View All or Modify All on the object bypass restriction rules entirely.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of using Login As to verify a security design, per Lesson 17, in the correct order.
items: Confirm 'Administrators Can Log In as Any User' is enabled under Login Access Policies
From Setup, open the Users list and find the active target user's row
Select Login next to that user's row to start a session as them
Navigate as that user, checking the specific records, fields, and buttons your design expects them to see
Log out of the impersonated session to return to your own
questions.explain: Lesson 17 lays this out as a deliberate sequence: confirm the policy allowing it, find the specific active user, start the impersonated session, verify the specific items your design predicts, then return to your own session — not a general-purpose way to browse as other people.

questions.prompt: This Apex test wraps its query and assertion inside System.runAs(rep). Why is that wrapping necessary to meaningfully test this rep's sharing access, instead of just running the query directly in the test method?
options: Apex normally executes in system context, which ignores sharing rules and field-level security entirely — System.runAs() is what makes the query actually run under the rep's real sharing restrictions
System.runAs() is required syntax any time a SOQL query appears inside an @isTest method, regardless of what's being tested
Without System.runAs(), the test would fail to compile, since System is a reserved context outside Apex tests
System.runAs() permanently changes which user is logged in for the rest of the org, so it must be reset afterward
questions.explain: Lesson 17 explains that Apex runs in system context by default, bypassing sharing and field-level security — a test written without System.runAs() could pass even though a real user would be blocked. Wrapping the query in System.runAs(rep) executes it under that specific user's actual sharing context.

questions.prompt: Match each access-checking tool from Lesson 18 to what it actually shows.
left: "Why am I able to see this?" sharing detail view
right: Lists every profile, permission set, and permission set group that grants access to a given object, from Object Manager
Directly confirms what a user experiences, once you already have a hypothesis to test
Shows exactly which rule, team, or hierarchy relationship grants a specific record's access
Shows every permission set, permission set group, and profile permission contributing to a user's access, in one place
questions.explain: The sharing detail view on a record shows exactly which rule or relationship grants access to that one record. A user's access summary shows every contributing permission set, group, and profile in one place. Object Manager's Object Access summary lists every source that grants access to an object. Login As is the tool that directly confirms what the user experiences, once you have a hypothesis to test.

questions.prompt: An org's sharing rules have grown to a dozen overlapping rules that collectively let nearly everyone see nearly everything. What does Lesson 19 say an admin should actually do?
options: Revisit the underlying OWD choice for that object, rather than add a thirteenth sharing rule
Grant View All instead, since it's simpler to maintain than a dozen rules
Convert every sharing rule into an equivalent permission set
Remove the role hierarchy, since the sharing rules have made it redundant
questions.explain: Lesson 19's Mistake 4 is exactly this pattern: sharing rules multiplying to cover most of the org is the signal to revisit the OWD choice itself, not to add rule number thirteen.

questions.prompt: In the Brightwell Insurance Group audit, which finding was prioritized to be fixed first, and why?
options: The missing restriction rule on Claim_Investigation__c, because it represented active, ongoing exposure of sensitive in-progress investigation data
The three near-identical Agent profiles, because consolidating profiles was the easiest fix to implement
The undocumented Modify All grant on five objects, because it was the easiest finding to explain to stakeholders
The Public Read/Write Opportunity OWD, because any OWD misconfiguration is automatically the top priority
questions.explain: Lesson 20 ranks findings by sensitivity of the data exposed and whether access is currently excessive, not by ease of fix — the Claim_Investigation__c gap was the most urgent because it was active, ongoing exposure of sensitive in-progress data, while the easiest fix (the profile explosion) was ranked lowest.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Salesforce precomputes who can see what in internal ________ tables, which must be rebuilt — recalculated — whenever something that feeds into them changes.
questions.explain: Lesson 21 explains that record access isn't computed fresh on every click — Salesforce maintains sharing tables behind the scenes, and recalculation is what keeps them in sync with OWD, the role hierarchy, and sharing rules as data and org structure change.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about sharing recalculation, per Lesson 21.
options: A user's role changing triggers automatic recalculation
Account, Opportunity, or Case ownership changing triggers automatic recalculation
A sharing rule's criteria or target group changing triggers automatic recalculation
Changing which fields a criteria-based sharing rule evaluates always recalculates automatically, with no exceptions
Large-scale structural changes, like a role-hierarchy redesign, can be triggered manually from the Sharing Settings page
questions.explain: Role changes, ownership changes, and sharing-rule edits all trigger automatic recalculation. Changing which fields a criteria-based rule evaluates requires manual recalculation in some cases, per the lesson — it isn't always automatic. Large structural changes can be triggered manually from Sharing Settings, typically timed for low-usage windows.

questions.prompt: A public Experience Cloud site's Guest User profile currently has Read access on Lead, left over from early development testing. The site's only Lead-related feature is a public lead-capture form. What should that access actually be, per Lesson 22?
options: Create only on Lead — the form only needs to insert new leads, not read any existing ones
Read and Create, since the guest user will eventually need to see submitted leads
View All on Lead, so anonymous visitors can audit each other's submissions
No change — guest user profiles don't need the same minimization discipline as internal profiles
questions.explain: Lesson 22 is explicit: a public lead-capture form needs Create on Lead, not Read — don't grant Read access just because it's convenient to test with. Start from nothing and add only what the site's actual functionality requires.

questions.prompt: Secure guest user record access has been mandatory since Summer '20 and can't be turned off. What does it actually require?
options: Record access for guest users must come from an explicit grant, such as a sharing rule or sharing set built for guest users — never implicitly from a permissive OWD
Every guest user must complete multi-factor authentication before a session can start
Guest users may be granted View All, but Modify All is permanently disabled for the Guest User profile
Every Experience Cloud site must generate a unique guest profile per visitor session
questions.explain: Lesson 22 describes Secure guest user record access as a platform-level floor: guest users no longer get implicit record access from a permissive OWD, and must instead get an explicit grant like a sharing rule or sharing set built specifically for them.

questions.prompt: Match each Session Settings concept to what it actually controls, per Lesson 23.
left: Lock sessions to the originating IP address
right: A required second verification factor beyond password, enforced org-wide on direct UI logins since 2022
How long an idle session stays valid before forcing re-authentication
A stronger authentication level required for specific sensitive actions, beyond a user's normal login
Prevents a stolen session token from being replayed from a different network
questions.explain: Session Timeout controls how long an idle session stays valid. Locking sessions to their originating IP stops a stolen token from being replayed elsewhere. High Assurance requires a stronger authentication level for specific sensitive actions. MFA is the required second factor at login, mandatory org-wide since 2022 — a different risk than anything session-related.

questions.prompt: An org requires MFA for every login but has a 24-hour session timeout and no IP locking. Is this org's login security and its session security the same thing?
options: No — MFA secures who is allowed to start a session, but a long timeout with no IP locking leaves an already-started session more exposed to hijacking or replay
Yes — MFA at login guarantees the session stays equally secure for its entire duration afterward
No — session timeout and IP locking are actually components of MFA itself, so this org hasn't truly enabled MFA
Yes, because Require HTTPS being on by default compensates for both gaps
questions.explain: Lesson 23 distinguishes login security (MFA, confirming who's logging in) from session security (timeout, IP locking, protecting an already-authenticated session). An org can have strong MFA and still leave the session itself under-protected — they're addressing different risks, not the same setting twice.
